lead: One kilogram block of ice left in a warm room takes in heat. It warms, then sits at 0 °C while it melts, then warms again, then sits at 100 °C while it boils. The same heat does three different jobs: raising temperature, pulling a phase apart, and — when a reaction runs — rearranging chemical bonds. Boiler design, refrigeration and every energy balance around a reactor need these three quantities kept separate. Add them wrongly and a plant's heat demand comes out wrong by a factor of five.
prereq: You need enthalpy and the first law from Unit 1, and Cp from Chapter 2.2.

blocks.text: Sensible heat is heat that changes the temperature of a substance. No phase change, no reaction. A thermometer shows the change, so the heat is called sensible.
Q = ∫ n Cp dT
blocks.where: Q is heat added (kJ); n is amount of substance (mol); Cp is molar heat capacity at constant pressure (kJ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹); T is absolute temperature (K).

blocks.text: When Cp is nearly constant over the range, the integral collapses to Q = n Cp (T₂ − T₁). Working in kilograms gives Q = m cp ΔT, where m is mass (kg), cp is specific heat capacity (kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹), and ΔT is the temperature change (K or °C — the size is the same).

Cp of a real gas climbs with temperature, so one number is only an average over the band. Use a mean Cp for the range, or fit Cp = a + bT + cT² and integrate term by term; Unit 4 shows where those fits come from.
Sign rule: Q is positive when heat enters the system. A 1 kg aluminium pressure cooker heated from 30 °C to 120 °C takes in 1 × 0.90 × 90 = 81 kJ before the food inside even warms.

sections.h3: Latent heat moves the molecules apart

blocks.text: Latent heat is heat that changes the phase of a substance at constant temperature and constant pressure. Nothing warms; the attraction between molecules gives way.
Q = m Δh
blocks.where: m is mass (kg); Δh is the specific latent heat (kJ kg⁻¹): Δh_fus for melting, Δh_vap for boiling, Δh_sub for solid to vapour.

blocks.text: At 1 atm, for water, Δh_fus = 334 kJ/kg at 0 °C and Δh_vap = 2260 kJ/kg at 100 °C. Each pair belongs to its own pressure; at another pressure both the value and the transition temperature change.

The 2260 kJ/kg does two jobs. Roughly 170 kJ/kg pushes the atmosphere aside as the vapour expands — that is the PΔV part of ΔH = ΔU + PΔV. The rest raises internal energy by breaking hydrogen bonds. So a steam burn at 100 °C is far worse than a water burn at 100 °C.

sections.h3: Heat of reaction: constant pressure and constant volume

blocks.text: A reaction swaps one set of bonds for another, and the enthalpy difference leaves as heat. Run it in an open beaker at constant pressure and the measured heat is Qp = ΔH_rxn. Run it in a sealed bomb at constant volume and the measured heat is Qv = ΔU_rxn. Some syllabi call all of this heat effects accompanying chemical reactions.
ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g R T
blocks.where: Δn_g is moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants; R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; T is in K. Only gases are counted.

blocks.text: The standard heat of formation ΔH°f is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states at 1 bar. Elements in their standard state have ΔH°f = 0 by definition: O₂ gas, N₂ gas, and carbon as graphite, not diamond.
ΔH°rxn = Σ ν ΔH°f(products) − Σ ν ΔH°f(reactants)
blocks.where: ν are the stoichiometric coefficients from the balanced equation.

blocks.text: The heat of combustion follows the same pattern for burning: 1 mol of fuel burns completely in oxygen to CO₂ gas and liquid water. It is easier to measure than formation, so data tables are full of it.
Hess's law: enthalpy is a state function, so a reaction run in several steps releases the same total heat as one step. Add the ΔH of the steps, flipping the sign of any step you run backwards.

sections.h3: Kirchhoff's law: heats of reaction at other temperatures

blocks.text: Heats of reaction are tabulated at 298 K, but plants run hotter. Kirchhoff's law carries ΔH from one temperature to another.
ΔCp = Σ ν Cp(products) − Σ ν Cp(reactants)
blocks.where: ΔCp is the heat capacity change per mole of reaction (kJ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹), using the same ν as the balanced equation.

blocks.text: ΔH_T2 = ΔH_T1 + ΔCp (T2 − T1)
blocks.where: valid when ΔCp is constant; otherwise use ΔH_T2 = ΔH_T1 + ∫ΔCp dT from T1 to T2.

blocks.text: The physical reason is simple. Products and reactants warm up by different amounts, so the enthalpy gap between them drifts with temperature. Kirchhoff's law is just sensible heat applied to that gap.
Real fluids need real data: enthalpies along the ice-to-steam path come from steam tables, not constant cp. See Unit 4 for property tables, and add a residual term for gases far from ideal behaviour.

figure.caption: Each flat step is latent heat at a fixed temperature; each sloping stretch is sensible heat. Vaporization alone is 2260 of the 3073 kJ/kg.

spec.title: Enthalpy path: ice to steam
spec.aria: Enthalpy–temperature path for 1 kg of water: sensible heating of ice to 0°C, a flat fusion step, sensible heating of liquid to 100°C, a flat vaporization step, then sensible heating of steam to 120°C; total 3073 kJ/kg.

examples.question: 1 kg of ice at −10 °C is heated at 1 atm until it becomes steam at 120 °C. Take cp,ice = 2.09 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, Δh_fus = 334 kJ/kg, cp,water = 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, Δh_vap = 2260 kJ/kg, cp,steam = 2.01 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Find the total heat supplied and the percentage of it that is latent heat.
steps: Step 1 — warm the ice from −10 °C to 0 °C: Q1 = m cp ΔT = 1 × 2.09 × 10 = 20.9 kJ.
Step 2 — melt the ice at 0 °C: Q2 = m Δh_fus = 1 × 334 = 334 kJ. Temperature stays at 0 °C.
Step 3 — warm the liquid water from 0 °C to 100 °C: Q3 = 1 × 4.18 × 100 = 418 kJ.
Step 4 — boil the water at 100 °C: Q4 = 1 × 2260 = 2260 kJ. Temperature stays at 100 °C.
Step 5 — superheat the steam from 100 °C to 120 °C: Q5 = 1 × 2.01 × 20 = 40.2 kJ.
Step 6 — add the five parts: Q_total = 20.9 + 334 + 418 + 2260 + 40.2 = 3073.1 kJ.
examples.answer: The total heat is 3073.1 kJ per kg, of which 2594 kJ (84.4 %) is latent heat.

traps: Adding latent heat at the wrong temperature: fusion belongs at 0 °C and vaporization at 100 °C only at 1 atm. At 2 atm the boiling term sits near 120 °C with a smaller Δh_vap.
Forgetting the sensible heat on one side of a phase change — the ice warming to 0 °C, or the steam superheating after 100 °C.
Mixing the molar and mass formulas: n Cp ΔT needs moles, m cp ΔT needs kilograms. Check units before you add the numbers.
Sign of ΔH: exothermic is negative, endothermic is positive. Write the sign in every line, not just the last one.
Using Qp = ΔH when the vessel is sealed: at constant volume the measured heat is ΔU, and ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT with T in kelvin and only gases counted in Δn_g.

quiz.q: Define sensible heat and give its SI unit.
quiz.a: Heat that changes the temperature of a substance without a phase change or a reaction; measured in joules (J).

quiz.q: State the latent heat of vaporization of water at 100 °C and 1 atm, with units.
Why does the temperature stay at 100 °C while water boils, even though heat keeps entering?
quiz.a: The energy goes into pulling molecules apart against their attraction — potential energy — not into the average kinetic energy that a thermometer reads.

quiz.q: 2 kg of water is heated from 25 °C to 75 °C. Take cp = 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Find Q.
A gas-phase reaction has ΔU = −50.0 kJ at 400 K with Δn_g = −2. Find ΔH.
Why does ΔH_rxn change with temperature at all? Where does the change come from?
quiz.a: Products and reactants have different heat capacities, so the enthalpy gap between them widens or narrows with temperature; the rate of change is ΔCp, which is Kirchhoff's law.

quiz.q: A student heating ice from −10 °C adds 2260 kJ/kg as the first step. Explain the error and give the correct order of steps.
quiz.a: 2260 kJ/kg is the latent heat of vaporization, valid at 100 °C, not for ice at −10 °C. Correct order: sensible heat of ice to 0 °C, fusion at 0 °C, sensible heat of water to 100 °C, vaporization at 100 °C, then sensible heat of steam.

quiz.q: State Hess's law and say why it holds.
quiz.a: The total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same however it is split into steps, because enthalpy is a state function and depends only on the initial and final states.

beyond: Not for the exam. Plant heat balances use steam tables and residual enthalpies instead of constant cp, and process simulators carry whole libraries of formation and combustion data. Pinch analysis uses these heat effects to pair hot and cold streams in a refinery so that utility steam is minimised. Heats of formation can also be computed rather than measured, by quantum-chemical methods, when a compound is too unstable to burn cleanly. Search for 'enthalpy of formation database', 'Kirchhoff equation' or 'pinch analysis' to go further.
